prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a new-onset seizure in an adult and focal neurological signs (right facial droop, right pronator drift, right extensor plantar response) are imaging-first criteria under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT delay empiric antibiotics and dexamethasone while awaiting CT or LP results beyond the 60-minute window; antibiotic delay beyond the first hour from clinical suspicion increases mortality.
Do NOT withhold dexamethasone because LP is pending; dexamethasone must precede or accompany the first antibiotic dose, even before the LP is performed.

Do NOT use inhaled corticosteroid use (COPD maintenance therapy) as a reason to classify the patient as significantly immunocompromised equivalent to systemic steroid therapy; empiric coverage should follow the standard adult community-acquired meningitis regimen.

Do NOT diagnose acute ischemic stroke with a post-ictal deficit without first considering bacterial meningitis in a febrile patient with meningismus, altered mental status and a focal seizure; fever and nuchal rigidity are not features of uncomplicated stroke.
required_recommendations: Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a new-onset seizure in an adult and focal neurological signs (right facial droop, right pronator drift, right extensor plantar response) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: S. pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.

Perform lumbar puncture as soon as CT has excluded mass effect; send cell count with differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis/encephalitis multiplex PCR and CSF lactate.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ceftriaxone alone for S. pneumoniae with ceftriaxone MIC 0.5 or less (penicillin MIC 0.12 is resistant by meningitis breakpoints); stop ampicillin and any vancomycin.
Treat this acute symptomatic seizure: give a benzodiazepine for any recurrence and start an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam; consider continuous EEG if consciousness does not improve.
If the right-sided deficit persists beyond the post-ictal period, obtain contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain to look for infarction, cerebritis, abscess or subdural empyema.
Place on droplet precautions until Neisseria meningitidis is excluded.
Monitor serum sodium closely; baseline hyponatremia likely reflects SIADH complicating the CNS infection.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis; no cardiac arrhythmia is suspected as a primary driver.
No clinical features of endocarditis (no murmur, no embolic stigmata); echocardiography is not part of the routine acute bacterial meningitis workup.
No specific arrhythmia indication; sinus tachycardia is expected in febrile sepsis and does not require dedicated cardiac monitoring in this context.
FDG-PET has no role in acute bacterial meningitis diagnosis or management.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool; it has no role in the workup of acute infectious meningitis.

differential.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke with a post-ictal deficit
differential.key_features: Focal seizure with right facial droop, pronator drift and extensor plantar can anchor toward a left-hemisphere stroke; fever 39.1 C, nuchal rigidity, bilateral meningeal signs and a purulent pneumococcal CSF are not explained by stroke, and the CT shows no infarct. Arterial ischemic complications of the meningitis remain possible if the deficit persists.

The focal seizure explains part of the transient right-sided deficit and confusion, but not the fever that preceded the seizure, the meningism or the CSF; it is a component of the presentation, not the diagnosis.
Focal seizure and encephalopathy fit HSV encephalitis; excluded by neutrophilic CSF with a glucose ratio of 0.17, Gram-positive diplococci, S. pneumoniae on PCR and HSV-1/2 not detected.
Lymphocyte-predominant CSF with near-normal glucose would be expected; the neutrophilic CSF, glucose ratio of 0.17 and S. pneumoniae exclude it.
Focal deficit and seizure could suggest abscess; non-contrast CT shows no mass, edema or midline shift. Contrast MRI is indicated if the focal deficit persists.
Subacute course, lymphocytic CSF and basal enhancement would be expected; excluded by the 1-day course, neutrophilic CSF and S. pneumoniae on PCR and blood culture.

key_clinical_evidence: Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a new-onset seizure in an adult and focal neurological signs (right facial droop, right pronator drift, right extensor plantar response) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
A CT without mass effect, midline shift or basal cistern effacement allows lumbar puncture; a normal CT neither diagnoses nor excludes meningitis.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

The focal right-sided seizure and motor deficit create a powerful stroke-anchoring trap: a naive workup focused on stroke would delay the CT, lumbar puncture and empirical treatment of a time-critical CNS infection.

Neutrophilic pleocytosis with a CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.17, protein of 284 mg/dL and Gram-positive diplococci establish bacterial meningitis; multiplex PCR and blood culture identify S. pneumoniae.
Inhaled corticosteroid use in COPD is not equivalent to systemic immunosuppression and does not independently mandate CT before LP; her new seizure and focal signs do.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Focal deficits and seizure in the setting of fever (39.1 C) and marked nuchal rigidity require meningitis to be urgently excluded. The new seizure and focal signs are WHO 2025 section A.4 imaging-first criteria: they mandate CT before LP and do not permit deferring LP or antibiotics.
red_herrings.data_point: Focal right-sided motor seizure with right pronator drift and right extensor plantar response
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the workup toward acute ischemic stroke (left MCA territory) or a primary seizure disorder as the diagnosis, diverting from meningitis evaluation and empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parameningeal sinus disease is a recognized source of hematogenous or direct spread of Streptococcus pneumoniae to the meninges, not an alternative diagnosis. The presence of sinusitis increases the probability of pneumococcal meningitis as the mechanism.
red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral maxillary and left ethmoid sinus mucosal thickening on CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest uncomplicated sinusitis as the primary diagnosis explaining fever, headache, and focal deficits, deferring the meningitis workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia in this context most likely reflects SIADH as a CNS-mediated complication of bacterial meningitis itself. Seizure threshold is lowered by hyponatremia, but the primary driver is the CNS infection — treat the underlying meningitis.
red_herrings.data_point: Hyponatremia (sodium 128 mEq/L) on admission chemistry panel
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect attention toward SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, or volume-depletion workup as the primary cause of confusion and seizure.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a new-onset seizure in an adult and focal neurological signs (right facial droop, right pronator drift, right extensor plantar response). NICE NG240 1.4.7 agrees (new focal neurological features). Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Patricia Holt is a 64-year-old right-handed White woman with a history of COPD on inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta-agonist therapy, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia who is brought to the emergency department by EMS after a witnessed focal seizure at home. Per her neighbor who called 911, Ms. Holt had been complaining of severe bifrontal headache and neck pain since yesterday morning, and appeared increasingly confused and disoriented throughout the day. She reportedly told her neighbor she "couldn't think straight" and was "burning up." This evening, the neighbor witnessed Ms. Holt suddenly develop rightward head turning and right arm tonic posturing lasting approximately 90 seconds, followed by secondary generalization with bilateral convulsions, which terminated spontaneously. The neighbor denied any prior history of seizures, head trauma, or similar episodes. EMS found Ms. Holt post-ictally confused with a temperature of 38.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate of 114, blood pressure of 152/88, and oxygen saturation of 91% on room air. She was administered supplemental oxygen en route. She did not receive any anticonvulsants prehospital.

On arrival in the ED, Ms. Holt remains markedly confused and disoriented. She is unable to provide meaningful history. Review of her medication bottles confirms current use of inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol and tiotropium for COPD, amlodipine, and rosuvastatin. She has never received pneumococcal vaccination. There is no family member present. The neighbor reports no recent antibiotic use, no sick contacts, no recent travel, and no prior neurological conditions. No immunodeficiency is recorded; her COPD is managed with inhaled corticosteroids.

On examination she has marked nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, severe photophobia, a subtle right facial droop, right pronator drift, and an extensor plantar response on the right.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked nuchal rigidity: passive neck flexion severely limited, patient grimaces and resists. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign positive. History from EMS: witnessed focal right-sided motor seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds with secondary generalization, terminating spontaneously en route to the ED. No papilledema on fundoscopic examination. No petechiae or skin rash. No evidence of head trauma.

Hearing grossly intact to finger snap bilaterally. Gag reflex intact. Tongue midline without fasciculations.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Markedly confused and disoriented. Oriented only to person; unable to state month, year, or location despite repeated prompting. GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5). Intermittently agitated, alternating with periods of somnolence. Does not follow commands reliably; intermittently follows one-step commands. Speech is disorganized with paraphasic substitutions.
